design_detail: 'Insights' commentary in European Neuropsychopharmacology (vol. 70, 2023, pp. 19-20; received 8 January, revised 31 January, accepted 2 February 2023) by Santiago Madero (Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, IDIBAPS) and Oscar D. Alvarez (Parc Sanitari Sant Joan de Deu), on the premise, promise and challenges of MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) for PTSD. Six paragraphs of running text (three beginning on p. 19, three on p. 20; paragraph numbers in the locators count from the start of the piece), 10 references, no tables, figures or new data. Written after the first phase 3 trial was published and before the second was (the second is described from the sponsor's top-line announcement).
can_establish: What two Spanish clinicians, one of them a principal investigator in the sponsor's trials, argued in early 2023 about MAPP1, the sponsor's regulatory plans, the risks of MDMA-assisted therapy, how it should be delivered, and its cost-effectiveness.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy works or is safe: no data are presented, the first trial is summarized in one sentence without numbers beyond 'as much as two thirds', and the safety, regulatory and economic statements are unreferenced or second-hand.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The trial cited (Mitchell et al., 2021) is described as the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site phase 3 trial, in patients with severe PTSD; no sample size is given.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen to support the argument: the first trial, a treatment manual and a review by the sponsor's investigators (Mithoefer, 2017; Sessa et al., 2019), a favourable modelling study (Avanceña et al., 2022) and a favourable review (Gonda et al., 2022). Two critical pieces (Yaden et al., 2022; Hall and Humphreys, 2022) are cited in one paragraph without detail. The second phase 3 trial is described from the sponsor's announcement, without a reference.

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not given. The piece describes MDMA-AT as sessions with MDMA, in an optimal setting with non-directive therapists, preceded by preparation and followed by integration sessions (p. 20, 4th paragraph); no doses or numbers of sessions are stated.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The trial's comparison is given as placebo, without saying that both arms received the same therapy.

outcomes.instruments: CAPS-5 is named as the trial's measure; no scores are given.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No longer meeting criteria for PTSD after completing treatment' is given for 'as much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm, without a denominator, a time point or the corresponding figure for the placebo arm.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed: blinding, expectancy and functional unblinding are not mentioned.

analysis.effect_sizes: None from the trial, beyond 'as much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria. The economic figures are second-hand model outputs (Avanceña et al., 2022): with access for 25-75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD over 10 years, 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted, 3.3-8.2 million quality-adjusted life years gained and 109 to 266 billion US dollars in net savings for the US health-care system.
analysis.selective_reporting: The safety statement (no adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation) has no citation and does not say how such events were assessed. The second phase 3 trial is reported only as announced top-line results meeting primary and secondary endpoints, without a reference. The model's assumptions (comparator, drug price) are not mentioned.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The piece summarizes the first trial's direction of effect in one sentence (a significant CAPS-5 reduction compared with placebo; up to two thirds of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria) and relays the sponsor's announcements about the second trial and its regulatory plans.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors write that approval by the FDA was very likely within the next year and a half (p. 19) and that the phase 2 and 3 trials have shown MDMA might revolutionize PTSD treatment, with benefits beyond all existing pharmacotherapies (p. 20, citing a review); in August 2024 the FDA rejected the application (Mahase, 2024). The safety profile is called favourable because the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation, without a source and without saying how these were recorded. Modelled projections of deaths averted and money saved are presented as what an analysis shows. The final paragraph warns of a hype bubble and of debate over lowered standards in major journals publishing psychedelic trials, without applying either concern to the trials it describes.

timeline.event: FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for the sponsor's programme, based on pooled phase 2 data, as stated by the commentary.
MAPP1, the first phase 3 trial (Mitchell et al., 2021).
Avanceña, Kahn and Marseille (2022), modelling study of expanded access to MDMA-assisted therapy in the USA, cited for the economic figures (not read).
This commentary (accepted 2 February 2023), citing the second phase 3 trial only from top-line results.
MAPP2, the second phase 3 trial, published later in 2023 (Mitchell et al., 2023).
The BMJ reports that the FDA rejected the application and that Psychopharmacology retracted three phase 2 analyses (Mahase, 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: The forecast of FDA approval within about 18 months of early 2023 was not borne out (Mahase, 2024). The European phase 3 trial planned for 2024 and a possible EMA approval from 2026 are forecasts whose outcome is not covered by the sources read here.

funding.declared_conflicts: O.A. is a principal investigator for the phase IIB and III clinical trials in the MAPS-sponsored MDMA-AT trials for PTSD and reports no other conflicts; S.M. reports none.
funding.affiliations_note: Santiago Madero: University Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, Psychiatry and Psychology Department, Bipolar and Depressive Disorders Unit, IDIBAPS; Oscar D. Alvarez: Parc Sanitari Sant Joan de Deu Hospital, Sant Joan de Deu Research Foundation. One author is an investigator in the trial programme whose results the piece summarizes. The economic figures come from a model whose authors include Elliot Marseille, who in 2025 declares consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos (Marseille and Mitchell, 2025, p. 3). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: The peer-reviewed trial reports read in full, with blinding, expectancy and adverse-event recording examined; independent replication; the regulator's own review documents; and, for the economic claims, models that use a standard-of-care comparator and realistic prices, with their assumptions published.

domains.note: A short commentary; no search, and sources chosen to support the argument.
Neither the trial nor the cost model is appraised; the safety statement and the second trial's results are unreferenced.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 10 references is by the authors; one author's role as a trial investigator is declared (see funding).
Regulatory forecasts, a mechanistic metaphor (the helioscope) and modelled projections sit beside the trial result as if of the same standing.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the benefits and risks of MDMA-assisted therapy (limitations of the trials under-represented)
domains.note: Risks, therapist training, hype and lowered journal standards are acknowledged, but no specific limitation of the trials is named.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The piece may be cited for what its authors argued and forecast in early 2023, including their recommendations on certified centres, screening and therapist training. It is not evidence on efficacy, blinding or adverse events, and its economic figures are second-hand model outputs.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime prevalence of PTSD is given as 1.3% to 12% depending on the population studied (Shalev et al., 2017; second-hand).

History as told by the authors: Merck developed MDMA in 1912; Alexander Shulgin resynthesized it in 1976; hundreds of therapists then gave MDMA and saw patients make, in a few sessions, progress that normally took years (no citation); it spread to the night scene as ecstasy; in October 1986 the DEA classified it in Schedule I, which the authors say was done without convincing academic arguments, and research was then hugely restricted.
key_findings.note: Nutt and de Wit (2021, p. 951) date the criminalization to 1985; see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: MAPS has led clinical research of MDMA-AT since the early 2000s; pooled data from all MAPS-sponsored phase 2 trials led to the FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation in 2017 and to multi-site phase 3 trials.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: MAPP1 (2021), described as the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site phase 3 trial in severe PTSD, is said to show a significant reduction in CAPS-5 score compared with placebo, with as much as two thirds of patients in the MDMA arm no longer meeting criteria for PTSD after completing treatment.
key_findings.note: No denominator, time point or placebo-arm figure is given; to be checked against the trial report (other first reader).

key_findings.finding: The authors write that the safety profile of MDMA appears favourable because the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation; no source is cited and the way these events were assessed is not described.

The sponsor had completed the second phase 3 trial (USA, Canada, Israel) and announced positive top-line results meeting its primary and secondary endpoints (no reference); it planned to submit a new drug application in the third quarter of 2023, and the authors judged approval very likely within the next year and a half. MAPS had trained therapists in seven European countries (Netherlands, Czech Republic, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Norway and England) for a phase 3 trial to start in 2024, and EMA approval might follow as early as 2026.

Proposed mechanism and delivery: sessions in an optimal setting with non-directive therapists, preceded by preparation and followed by integration; the pharmacological and subjective effects of MDMA are said to impair the fear response selectively while leaving other cognitive processes relatively spared (Mithoefer, 2017; Sessa et al., 2019); Hasler's 'helioscope' hypothesis (2022) is offered as a model of how psychedelics let people look at what they otherwise could not.

Risks: MDMA-AT has inherent risks, which the authors say increase in recreational settings (abuse potential, triggering of psychiatric disorders, especially in people with pre-existing vulnerabilities such as psychotic disorders). They recommend that after approval administration be limited to certified centres with defined safety screening and a centralized pharmacy, with trained therapists under supervision, and name therapist training as probably the main limit on availability.

Economic figures quoted from a modelling study (Avanceña et al., 2022): increasing access to MDMA-AT to 25-75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD over 10 years could avert 43,000 to 106,000 deaths, gain 3.3-8.2 million quality-adjusted life years and save 109 to 266 billion US dollars net for the US health-care system.
key_findings.note: Model outputs, second-hand; the model's comparator and price assumptions are not given.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that the phase 2 and 3 findings show MDMA might revolutionize the treatment of PTSD, with benefits beyond all current pharmacotherapies (Gonda et al., 2022), and cite a scientometric analysis showing a trend toward clinical testing of MDMA, psilocybin and ketamine with psychotherapy (Solmi et al., 2022).

They add that psychedelic research appears to be caught in a hype bubble driven largely by media and industry interests (Yaden et al., 2022) and that there has been debate over major medical journals lowering their standards for psychedelic trials (Hall and Humphreys, 2022), a combination they say could prove disastrous unless research keeps the highest ethical and scientific standards.
Declaration of competing interest: O.A. is a principal investigator for the phase IIB and III MAPS-sponsored MDMA-AT trials for PTSD; S.M. declares none.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation has no citation and does not say how such events were looked for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used as evidence on adverse events; the trial report and the critiques of its adverse-event recording are needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The second phase 3 trial's results are reported from the sponsor's top-line announcement, without a reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the published trial report (Mitchell et al., 2023) instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary dates Schedule I classification of MDMA by the DEA to October 1986; Nutt and de Wit (2021, p. 951) date its criminalization to 1985. Neither cites a scheduling document.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates of US scheduling should come from the legal-status sources (section 13).

reporting_issues.issue: 'As much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria is given without a denominator, a time point or the placebo-arm figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a remission rate; the absolute difference between arms must come from the trial report.

reporting_issues.issue: Modelled projections (deaths averted, quality-adjusted life years, net savings) are presented as what a recent analysis shows, without the model's comparator or price assumptions.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are model outputs, not observed outcomes; see the cost-effectiveness critique (Marseille and Mitchell, 2025) for what such results depend on.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 19-20 (PDFs/MDMA/Madero_2023_PremisePromiseChallenges.pdf): read in full, including the declaration of competing interest and the reference list; both pages rendered.
